title: Password hashing: why SHA256 is wrong and bcrypt/argon2 are right
story:
A general-purpose hash is one-way, which is the property people remember, and fast, which is the property that matters here. Speed is not an accident of implementation — it is a design requirement for the jobs those functions exist to do, like checking a file has not changed or verifying a signature. You want those to be as quick as the hardware allows.

Store a password with one and consider what you have actually arranged. Verifying a login costs one hash. Testing a guess also costs one hash. The defender and the attacker are charged exactly the same price for the same operation, and the attacker performs the operation an enormous number of times on hardware chosen for throughput. There is no asymmetry anywhere in the design, and the security of the scheme rests entirely on the attacker never obtaining the stored hashes — which is the one event the hashing was supposed to survive.

So the requirement is not a better one-way function. It is a function where the defender sets the price.

Niels Provos and David Mazières presented A Future-Adaptable Password Scheme at the 1999 USENIX Annual Technical Conference. Their scheme, based on the Blowfish cipher, takes a cost parameter which sets how much work hashing a password requires — and the point of the parameter is in the title. The cost can be raised over time as hardware gets faster, without changing the algorithm and without invalidating hashes already stored. That is the actual contribution, and it is a claim about the future rather than about the present: any fixed cost is eventually cheap, so the only scheme that survives is one whose cost is a dial.

The next move was to make the dial control something other than time. The Password Hashing Competition ran from 2013 to 2015 to select a new password hashing function, in the manner of the earlier open competitions for block ciphers and hash functions, and selected Argon2 in 2015.

Argon2 is memory-hard, and the reason that matters is worth following rather than accepting. Making a function slow in time is defeated by parallelism: an attacker who cannot make a single guess faster simply makes many guesses at once, and specialised hardware is very good at replicating small arithmetic units. Making it expensive in memory attacks that directly, because every guess in flight must hold its own memory as well as its own arithmetic. Silicon area spent on memory is area not spent on more guessing units, so the attacker's parallelism advantage is bounded by something he cannot simply buy more cheaply. Argon2 is defined in three variants — Argon2d, Argon2i and Argon2id — which differ in how they access memory and so in their resistance to side-channel observation.

The salt is a separate mechanism solving a separate problem, and conflating the two is the usual error. A salt is a unique random value stored alongside each hash, not secret. It does not slow anything down. What it does is destroy the economics of attacking many accounts at once: without one, a single guess can be tested against every user in the database simultaneously, and precomputed tables of common passwords work against everybody. With one, each stored hash has to be attacked separately, so the attacker's cost scales with the number of accounts rather than being amortised across them. Slowness raises the price of one guess; salting stops one guess from counting as many.

The cost is real and lands on the defender. Every login now performs the work the attacker was meant to be charged, which makes an unauthenticated login endpoint a way to spend the server's processor time — so a cost parameter chosen without rate limiting converts a password-cracking defence into an availability problem. And the parameter has no correct value: it depends on the hardware you have, the hardware the attacker has, and how long you need the stored hashes to remain valuable, which is the rest of their lifetime rather than the rest of yours.

One caution about the numbers that circulate. Specific cracking rates are quoted constantly and they are stale by construction — they describe one consumer graphics card at one moment and are wrong within a year in a direction that favours the attacker. The durable statement is structural: a general-purpose hash is as fast as the hardware permits and gets faster every generation, so it is not a question of whether a given card is fast enough today.

problem.name: The defender sets the price
problem.shape: A password must be stored so that stealing the store does not yield the passwords.
tell: a general-purpose hash is used for passwords
the work factor was chosen once and never revisited
two users with the same password have the same stored value
the login endpoint has no rate limit
problem.move: Use a function with a tunable cost, set it as high as the login path can bear, and revisit it as hardware improves. Salt each password with a unique random value so that no guess counts against more than one account, and rate-limit authentication because the cost you imposed is now also yours.
problem.invariant: With a general-purpose hash the defender and the attacker pay the same price per operation, and the attacker performs vastly more of them. Security requires a price the defender can raise and the attacker cannot lower.
problem.breaks: Any cost chosen today is cheap eventually, which is why adaptability rather than slowness is the property that matters — and hashes stored under an old parameter keep that parameter until each user next logs in. So raising the cost protects new passwords immediately and old ones only gradually, and a dormant account never upgrades at all.

cost.time: the work factor is charged to every legitimate login, so the login path becomes a way to consume server processor time unless it is rate-limited
cost.space: memory-hard functions consume substantial memory per concurrent authentication, which is a capacity planning input rather than a footnote
cost.beats: a general-purpose hash, which is fast for everyone including the attacker, and an external authentication provider, which removes the problem and adds a dependency and a different class of compromise

worked.problem: What is a salt, and which specific attack does it neutralise?
worked.reasoning:
A salt is a unique random value generated per password, stored in the clear alongside the hash, and mixed with the password before hashing. It is not secret, and it does not make anything slower — which is exactly why it has to be understood as a separate mechanism from the work factor rather than a part of it.

What it removes is the amortisation of an attack across accounts. Without a salt, the stored value is a function of the password alone, so identical passwords produce identical stored values. Two consequences follow, and both are about scale rather than about any individual password. First, a single guess can be hashed once and compared against every row in the database at the same time, so attacking a million accounts costs almost exactly what attacking one costs. Second, the table of hashes for common passwords can be computed in advance, before any breach, by anyone, and reused against every system that uses the same function.

A unique salt per password breaks both, because the stored value is now a function of the password and that user's salt. The precomputed table is useless, since it would have to be recomputed per salt. And each account must be attacked separately, so the attacker's total cost scales with the number of accounts instead of being amortised over them.

The division of labour is the thing to state clearly, because these get conflated: the work factor raises the price of a single guess; the salt stops a single guess from counting as many. Neither substitutes for the other. A slow hash without salts still lets one guess be tested against everybody at once. Salts with a fast hash still let each account fall quickly, just individually.

Which is the context for why slowness alone stopped being sufficient. Making a function slow in time is answered by parallelism — an attacker who cannot make one guess faster makes many at once, and specialised hardware replicates small arithmetic units very cheaply. Memory hardness attacks that directly: every guess in flight must hold its own memory as well as its own arithmetic, and silicon spent on memory is silicon not spent on more guessing units. That is what Argon2 provides, and why the competition that selected it in 2015 was looking for more than a slower hash.

The underlying requirement, stated once, is the one from the 1999 paper that introduced the cost parameter: the scheme has to be future-adaptable. Any fixed cost is eventually cheap, so the property that matters is not that the function is slow but that its cost is a dial the defender can turn as hardware improves — without changing the algorithm and without invalidating stored hashes.

I would add the limitation that follows from that, because it is rarely mentioned. A stored hash keeps whatever parameter it was created with until the user next logs in and it can be recomputed. So raising the work factor protects new passwords immediately and old ones only gradually, and a dormant account is still sitting behind whatever was considered adequate years ago.

problem.practice: Find the work factor your system uses and the date it was chosen. Then check whether anything re-hashes a password on successful login — if not, your oldest accounts are still protected at whatever level was considered adequate when they were created.

beats.broke: A general-purpose hash charges the defender and the attacker the same price per operation, and the attacker performs vastly more of them on hardware chosen for throughput — so the scheme relies on the stored hashes never being stolen, which is the event it existed to survive.
beats.fix: Use a function whose cost is a parameter the defender sets and can raise as hardware improves, and make the cost fall on memory as well as time so parallel hardware cannot simply buy its way around it.
beats.cost: Every legitimate login pays the work the attacker was meant to be charged, so an unrate-limited login endpoint becomes a way to spend the server's processor time.

interview.q: What is a cryptographic salt in password hashing, and what specific attack does it neutralise?
interview.trap: Describing the salt as making hashing slower or as a secret. It is neither — it is stored in the clear and costs nothing, and it solves amortisation across accounts rather than the price of a single guess.
interview.answer:
A salt is a unique random value generated per password, stored in the clear beside the hash and mixed with the password before hashing. It is not secret and it slows nothing down, which is why it has to be understood as separate from the work factor.

What it removes is the amortisation of an attack across accounts. Without one, the stored value is a function of the password alone, so identical passwords produce identical stored values. Two things follow, both about scale: a single guess can be hashed once and compared against every row at the same time, so attacking a million accounts costs about what attacking one costs; and tables of hashes for common passwords can be built in advance, by anyone, before any breach, and reused against every system using that function.

A unique salt breaks both, because the stored value now depends on the password and that user's salt. The precomputed table is useless, and each account must be attacked separately, so cost scales with the number of accounts rather than being amortised over them.

The division of labour is the part to say explicitly: the work factor raises the price of one guess, the salt stops one guess counting as many, and neither substitutes for the other. A slow hash without salts still lets one guess be tested against everybody at once; salts with a fast hash still let each account fall quickly, just individually.

That is also the context for memory hardness. Slowness in time is answered by parallelism, since specialised hardware replicates small arithmetic units cheaply. Memory hardness attacks that directly — every guess in flight must hold its own memory, and silicon spent on memory is not spent on more guessing units — which is what Argon2 provides and why the 2015 competition wanted more than a slower hash.

Underneath it all is the requirement from the 1999 paper that introduced the cost parameter: the scheme must be future-adaptable, because any fixed cost is eventually cheap. What matters is not that the function is slow but that its cost is a dial, raisable without changing the algorithm or invalidating stored hashes.

And the limitation that follows is rarely mentioned: a stored hash keeps the parameter it was created with until the user next logs in, so raising the work factor protects new passwords immediately and old ones only gradually — and a dormant account never upgrades at all.
